title: The struggle against France for independence, 1945–54

review.note: Original content following 4HI1 Historical investigation A4, key topic 1. No class textbook uploaded for this option yet.

learn.intro: After the Second World War, Ho Chi Minh's Vietminh declared Vietnamese independence. France tried to take back its colony, leading to eight years of war that ended in French defeat at Dien Bien Phu.

sections.title: 1. Origins of the First Indochina War and the aims of the Vietminh

blocks.p: Vietnam had been part of French Indochina since the late 1800s. During the Second World War Japan occupied it. In 1941 Ho Chi Minh, a communist and nationalist, set up the Vietminh (League for the Independence of Vietnam) to fight the Japanese and the French.

When Japan surrendered, Ho declared Vietnamese independence in Hanoi on 2 September 1945, quoting the American Declaration of Independence. But France wanted its colony back. Talks failed, and after French ships shelled Haiphong in November 1946, full war began in December 1946.
The Vietminh's aims: full independence from France, a united Vietnam, land for peasants, and a communist government. Their message of independence and land reform won wide peasant support.

sections.title: 2. General Giap's tactics and the search for a solution

blocks.p: General Vo Nguyen Giap commanded the Vietminh army. Following Mao's ideas, he used guerrilla warfare: small units, ambushes, hit-and-run attacks and support from villagers, avoiding large battles while the French were stronger. The aim was to wear the French down and only fight conventional battles once strong enough.

After the communists won in China in 1949, the Vietminh received Chinese weapons, training and safe bases. The USA, fearing the spread of communism, paid an increasing share of France's war costs — by 1954 most of them.
France looked for a way out. Peace talks began at the Geneva Conference in April 1954, while the decisive battle was being fought.

evidence: 1949: communist victory in China brings aid to the Vietminh.
By 1954 the USA paid most of France's war costs.

sections.title: 3. Dien Bien Phu and its consequences

blocks.p: In November 1953 the French built a fortified base at Dien Bien Phu, in a valley near the Laos border, hoping to lure the Vietminh into a battle they would lose. Instead, Giap's forces dragged heavy artillery up the surrounding hills by hand and surrounded the base.

The siege began on 13 March 1954. Vietminh artillery destroyed the airstrip, so the French could only be supplied by parachute. The base surrendered on 7 May 1954, and thousands of French troops were captured.

Immediate consequences: France decided to leave Indochina. The Geneva Agreements (July 1954) recognised the independence of Vietnam, Laos and Cambodia and temporarily divided Vietnam at the 17th parallel — communist North under Ho, non-communist South — with national elections promised for 1956.

evidence: November 1953: French base at Dien Bien Phu.
July 1954: Geneva Agreements — division at the 17th parallel; elections promised for 1956.

flashcards.q: What were the aims of the Vietminh?
flashcards.a: Independence from France, a united Vietnam, land for peasants and a communist government.
Guerrilla warfare — small units, ambushes, hit-and-run, support from villagers; big battles only when strong enough.

flashcards.q: How did the USA help France?
flashcards.a: Paid an increasing share of the war costs — most of them by 1954.

flashcards.q: Why did the French lose at Dien Bien Phu?
flashcards.a: Base in a valley; Giap's artillery on the hills destroyed the airstrip; supply only by parachute.

flashcards.q: What did the Geneva Agreements decide?
flashcards.a: Independence for Vietnam, Laos and Cambodia; temporary division at the 17th parallel; elections in 1956.
